idiom_name: State interface (or abstract class) + concrete state classes + context setter
implementation_notes: Java's classic realization is a State interface, or an abstract class when states share behaviour, plus one final class per state and a context that keeps the current state in a field and delegates through a package-private setter. Stateless states are usually enum constants or static final singletons, and an enum whose constants implement an abstract method is a common variant that keeps state identity serializable for free. Dynamic dispatch replaces the state conditionals; the class-per-state form is still justified when states carry collaborators, need inheritance-based reuse, or when the code must run on Java 8.
pitfalls: Serializing the state object or its class name instead of a stable token breaks stored data when a state is renamed; prefer an enum constant or an explicit code.
static final state instances must be immutable - mutable shared state leaks between documents.
A public state setter lets any caller jump the state graph; keep it package-private or expose only named transitions.

variants.name: Sealed interface with records and an exhaustive pattern-matching switch
variants.idiom_name: sealed interface + records + switch over the state (Java 21)
variants.implementation_notes: With sealed interfaces, records and pattern matching (final in Java 21) the state set becomes a closed algebraic type: sealed interface Phase permits Draft, Published, one record per state, and a switch expression over the state that the compiler proves exhaustive without a default arm. States become immutable values that can be copied, compared and serialized, and transition logic can live in one pure method instead of being spread across state classes. Prefer this when the graph is data and the code targets Java 21 or later; keep the polymorphic form for dependency-carrying states or Java 8 targets.
pitfalls: Adding a default arm or an instanceof chain destroys the exhaustiveness guarantee; let the compiler report the missing case instead.
Permitted subclasses must live in the same module or package as the sealed interface, so states cannot be added by other modules.
Pattern variables are scoped to their arm, and records are immutable, so a modification means returning a new state value rather than mutating one.
